item.title: Republicans Let Trump Keep Unparalleled Benefit: I.R.S. Immunity
item.description: The rebellion against Todd Blanche’s nomination to be attorney general, now seemingly contained, at no point fundamentally questioned President Trump’s new protections from the I.R.S.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Duehren
item.media:credit: Doug Mills/The New York Times
item.media:description: President Trump no longer has to worry about the Internal Revenue Service coming after him for any of the many aggressive tax positions he has taken over the years.

item.title: Todd Blanche Wins Over G.O.P. Holdouts on AG Confirmation After Assurances on Trump IRS Deal
item.description: Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis expressed support after Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, issued a memo abandoning part of a deal the Justice Department had struck with President Trump.
item.dc:creator: Michael Gold and Andrew Duehren
item.media:credit: Kenny Holston/The New York Times
item.media:description: Todd Blanche speaking at the Capitol last month.

item.title: Trump’s Meddling in Justice Dept. Causes Problems of His Own Making
item.description: In the past week alone, President Trump’s interference has imperiled one criminal case, set the stage for sanctions in a second and hindered the confirmation chances of his pick for attorney general.
item.dc:creator: Alan Feuer
item.media:credit: Pete Marovich for The New York Times
item.media:description: President Trump has long believed that he enjoys complete control over the agencies beneath him, including the Justice Department.

item.title: Documents Undercut Trump’s Claims About Bears Ears National Monument
item.description: President Trump said recreation in Bears Ears National Monument was virtually impossible. Documents reviewed by The New York Times show officials knew otherwise.
item.dc:creator: Maxine Joselow
item.media:credit: Alex Goodlett for The New York Times
item.media:description: The sun rises over Valley of The Gods inside Bears Ears National Monument in 2017 near Blanding, Utah.

item.title: For Trump, the Year Is Always 2020
item.description: President Trump insists on revisiting and rewriting much of what happened six years ago, including the coronavirus pandemic and the election he lost. Many voters would rather he focus on 2026.
item.dc:creator: Katie Rogers
item.media:credit: Doug Mills/The New York Times
item.media:description: Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, center, with President Trump, left, for a daily coronavirus pandemic briefing in 2020.

item.title: Education Dept. to Wipe Out Student Loans of 170,000 More Defrauded Borrowers
item.description: The sprawling case, centered on students defrauded by for-profit schools, has now become the largest class-action settlement in American history.
item.dc:creator: Stacy Cowley
item.media:credit: Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group, via Getty Images
item.media:description: Kaplan College was one of the more than 150 institutions, mostly for-profit colleges, named in the 2022 settlement in the case.

item.title: Prosecutor in D.C. Moves to Dismiss More Reflecting Pool Cases
item.description: After revelations that a botched renovation, not vandalism, had caused the pool’s recent problems, the U.S. attorney’s office has dropped several prosecutions.
item.dc:creator: Clarence Williams
item.media:credit: Andrew Leyden for The New York Times
item.media:description: The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington in July.

item.title: Author of Democrats’ 2024 Autopsy Says Party Left Out Key Chapter
item.description: A dispute over the chapter between the author and the Democratic National Committee has added to the party’s turmoil as it tries to look forward, not backward.
item.dc:creator: Shane Goldmacher
item.media:credit: Kent Nishimura for The New York Times
item.media:description: The Democratic National Committee’s autopsy of the 2024 election was meant to examine missteps that led to the party’s defeat.

item.title: In Michigan’s 7th District’s Democratic Primary, a Centrist Split Boosts Progressive Hopes
item.description: Unable to unite behind a single candidate in Michigan’s Seventh Congressional District, moderate Democrats worry that they’ve complicated their chances in a key November battleground.
item.dc:creator: Evan Gorelick
item.media:credit: Matt Maasdam For Congress; Nathan Layne/Reuters; William Lawrence for U.S. Congress
item.media:description: Matt Maasdam, Bridget Brink and Will Lawrence.

item.title: How Democratic Socialists Are Wrestling With Their Next Moves
item.description: After notching primary victories, D.S.A. members in Chicago debated whether socialist candidates should be free to distance themselves from goals like abolishing prisons as they chase more seats this fall.
item.dc:creator: Kellen Browning
item.media:credit: Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times
item.media:description: Ashik Siddique, a national chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, spoke to attendees at Maria’s Packaged Goods & Community Bar at a party on Friday after the group’s summit.

item.title: California Democrats Want to Tax Billionaires. They Can’t Agree on How.
item.description: Leaders of the state Democratic Party endorsed the ballot measure slated for November, but the party remains far from united on the issue as Democrats nationwide grapple with a growing wealth gap.
item.dc:creator: Laurel Rosenhall and Soumya Karlamangla

item.title: Immigrant Held at Delaney Detention Center Has Died, Officials Say
item.description: The mayor of Newark identified the dead man as Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo. The New Jersey center has been the focus of intense scrutiny for its treatment of detainees.
item.dc:creator: Ana Ley, Tracey Tully and Mark Bonamo
item.media:credit: Madison Swart for The New York Times
item.media:description: A man died at the Delaney Hall detention center in Newark over the weekend.

item.title: ICE Killed Him. A.I. Helped Turn Him Into a Folk Ballad, Fast.
item.description: Artificial Intelligence is helping people write corridos within hours, accelerating a century-old tradition of memorializing tragedy through song.
item.dc:creator: Sasha von Oldershausen and Antranik Tavitian

item.title: N.Y. Law Barring ICE Agents From Wearing Masks Is Blocked by Judge
item.description: While the ruling dealt a blow to New York’s efforts to rein in ICE, a ban on formal cooperation with local police officers will move forward.
item.dc:creator: Grace Ashford
item.media:credit: Madison Swart for The New York Times
item.media:description: Agents working for ICE typically wear face coverings, making it difficult to identify them in cases where they may have overstepped their authority.

item.title: Nanit and Other Baby-Tracking Start-Ups Eye Collecting Even More Data
item.description: Nanit and other start-ups want to track your children through the night — and soon, for much longer than that.
item.dc:creator: Sapna Maheshwari
item.media:credit: Photo illustration by Margeaux Walter for The New York Times
item.media:description: Young parents are increasingly willing to embrace tracking and analytics for their children — part of a broader cultural obsession with health data and optimization.

item.title: Senate Moves Ahead on Bill to Avert a Shutdown

item.media:description: The U.S. Capitol last week.

item.title: House Ethics Panel Finds Rep. Chuck Edwards Likely Violated Sexual Harassment Rules

item.title: Brown’s President Will Resign after a Tenure that Included Trump Deal
item.description: The president, Christina H. Paxson, led the campus for over a decade, but in recent years faced protests, political pressure and a shooting that killed two students.

item.title: After Colleges Reject ‘Compact,’ Trump Officials Try a Letter
item.description: The open letter from Education Secretary Linda McMahon fell far short of the attempt at a compact last year that dangled research money in return for embracing the Trump administration’s agenda.
item.dc:creator: Michael C. Bender and Alan Blinder
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times
item.media:description: Linda McMahon, the education secretary, signed the letter that asks every postsecondary institution in the nation to publicly state its commitments and planned changes “before the end of 2026.”

item.title: The German Auto Industry, a Pillar of the National Psyche, Is Trembling
item.description: The country’s iconic carmakers are struggling with tariffs, the growth of electric vehicles and intense competition from Chinese companies.

item.title: Gen Z Can’t Afford a First Date
item.description: From $130 dinners to expensive cocktails and even exorbitant movie tickets, a crushing economy in New York City is creating a fresh barrier to love.
item.dc:creator: Troy Closson
item.media:credit: Gary Hershorn/Getty Images
item.media:description: People in their 20s and 30s are dating less than earlier generations did. The high cost of going out is one of the reasons.

item.title: SpaceX’s Stock Lockup Is Expiring. Prepare for a Bumpy Ride.
